OBITUARY REFERENCE 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, I refer with profound sorrow to the 
passing away of Shri Bhagwan Din, a former Member of this House on the 
18th February, 2002, at Lucknow, at the age of 85. 
Born at Kanpur city in April, 1916, Shri Bhagwan Din had his education at 
Kanpur. A dedicated social and political worker Shri Bhagwan Din was 
associated with several social welfare organizations and worked for the uplift 
of the downtrodden. He was Vice-President of the All India Depressed 
Classes League in 1947, and the Bhartiya Safai Federation (erstwhile All 
India Sweepers Labour Federation) in 1948. 
The legislative career of Shri Bhagwan Din started with membership of the 
Uttar Pradesh Legislative Assembly from 1946 to 1952 and, again, from 1952 
to 1957. He was also a Member of the Constituent Assembly from 1946 to 
1950. He represented the State of Uttar Pradesh in this House from April, 
1976 to April, 1982. 
In the passing away of Shri Bhagwan Din, the country has lost a veteran 
parliamentarian and an active social worker. 
We deeply mourn the passing away of Shri Bhagwan Din. 
I request members to rise in their places and observe silence as a mark of 
respect to the memory of the departed. 
(Hon. Members then stood in 'silence for one minute) 
MR. CHAIRMAN: The Secretary-General will convey to the members of 
the bereaved family our deep sense of sorrow and sympathy.

Prime Minister's Japan Visit 
*262. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of 
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Prime Minister's visit to Japan has been successful; 
(b) if so, whether Japan has agreed to provide aid that was stopped due to 
the Pokhran test; 
(c) to what extent Japanese investment in India would increase; and 
(d) if so, to what extent these agreements would help? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Economic sanctions imposed by Japan after India's nuclear tests in 
May, 1998 were unilaterally lifted by the Government of Japan on 26 
October, 2001. 
(c) and (d) Prime Ministers of both countries acknowledged that broad 
and deepened economic relations are an essential underpinning to further 
strengthen bilateral relations. They shared the view that India's continuing 
economic reforms, recovery of the Ja panese economy through structural 
reform and the complementarities between the two economies will provide a 
solid foundation for further enhancing bilateral economic relations.

*263. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of 
LABOUR be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news- 
report captioned "Central labours to make lay-offs easy" which 
appeared in the 'Newstime dated the 23rd February, 2002; and 
(b) the safeguards taken/proposed to be taken to protect 
interests of labour before amending the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947 to lay off employees without Government's permission? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (SHRI SHARAD YADAV): (a) and (b) A 
statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Attention of the Government has been drawn to the news- 
item which appeared in the Newstime dated 23rd February, 2002. 
(b) Amendments to various labour laws are brought about 
keeping in view the re quirements of the social partners and after 
ensuring that the workers interest s are fully protected. The Hon'ble 
Finance Minister in his Budget  Speech in February, 2001 had 
indicated the Government's intention to amend the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947. It had been proposed in the said Budget 
Speech that the provisions of Chapter VB of the I.D. Act may 
now apply to the industrial establishments employing not less than 
7 

RAJYA SABHA [21 March, 2002] 
1000 workers instead  of  100  and  that the compensation will be increased 
from 15 day to 45 days for every completed year of service. 
At present sufficient safeguards to protect the interests of workmen during 
"lay-off" is provided under section 25 C of the I.D. Act, 1947 under which a 
workman is to be paid lay-off compensation equal to 50 per cent of the wages 
upto 45 days in a year by the employer. After lay-off, if a workman is 
retrenched, it shall be lawful for the employer to adjust the lay-off 
compensation paid to the workman against the compensation payable for 
retrenchment. The existing legal rights under the I.D. Act, 1947 provide that 
the workman shall be entitled to one month's notice in writing by the 
employer indicating the reasons for retrenchment and in lieu of such notice 
wages for the period of notice.

Uniform sugarcane price 
*267. SHRI NARENDRA  MOHAN: Will the Minister of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) the reasons for not having uniform sugarcane price all over the country 
as sugarcane itself is a major cost input in manufacturing sugar; and 
(b) if not, the administrative difficulties in doing so? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUMAR): (a) and (b) Under the 
provisions of the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1966, the Central Government 
fixes the Statutory Minimum Price (SMP) of sugarcane for each sugar season

growers. The basic SMP linked to 8.5% recovery is uniform. For every 0.1%

However, the SMP payable by the sugar factories varies from factory to 
factory depending upon the recovery level.

DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUM AR): (a) As on December 31,

The procurement operations are voluntary in nature and the farmers have

(b)   As   against  the  loss  of 4.49  lakh   tonnes  expected  during 
29

guarantee for the construction of 83.26 lakh tonnes storage capacity

Chairmanship of Prof. Abhijit Sen. The Committee is expected to submit its

following steps are being taken:

regular  stock verification;

curb theft and pilferage; 
(v) streamlining procedures and documentation for transparency and 
accountability in operations; 
(vi) regular and surprise inspection of depots by senior officers; 
(vii) improvement in size and quality of gunnies; 
(viii) augmentation of covered storage capacity; and 
(ix) introduction of bulk handling storage and transportation of foodgrains 
stocks.

periherals for electronic units under Export-Oriented schemes

Norms for opening post offices 
1. Norms for opening Extra Depa rtmental Branch Post Offices: 
1.1 Population: 
(a) In Normal Areas: 
3000 population in a group of villages (including the PPO village) 
(b) In Hilly, Tribal, Desert and Inaccessible Areas: 
500 population in an individual village or 1000 population in a group of 
villages. 
1.2 Distance: 
(a) In Normal Areas: 
The minimum distance from the nearest existing post office will be 3 Kms. 
(b) In Hilly, Tribal, Desert and Inaccessible Areas: 
The distance limit will be the same as above except that in Hilly Areas, the 
minimum distance limit can be relaxe d by the Directorate in cases where 
such relaxation is warranted by special circumstances which should be clearly 
explained while submitting a proposal. 
1.3 Anticipated Income: 
(a) In Normal Areas: 
The minimum anticipated revenue will be 33.1/3% of the cost. 
(b) In Hilly, Tribal, Desert and Inaccessible Areas: 
The minimum anticipated income will be 15% of the cost. 
2. Criteria for upgrading'opeiiing Departmental Sub Post Offices: 
(a) In Rural Areas: 
The minimum work load of the Extra Departmental Branch Post Office, 
proposed to be upgraded, shold be five hours per day. The permissible limit of 
annual loss is Rs. 2400 /- in Normal Rural areas and Rs. 4800 /- in Tribal and 
Hilly areas.

[21 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) In Urban Areas: 
In Urban areas, the post office should initially be self-supporting and at 
the time of the first annual review, it should show a 5% profit to be eligible 
for further retention. 
The minimum distance between two post offices should be 1.5 Kms. in 
cities with a population of 20 lakhs and above, and 2 Kms. in other Urban 
Areas. No two delivery offices, however, should be closer than 5 Kms. for 
each other. 
Heads of Circles have powers to relax the distance condition in 10% of 
the cases. 
A Delivery Post Office in Urban Area should have a minimum of 7 
Postmen's beats.

Diversion of foodgrains from TPDS 
1952. SHRI SURESH PA CHOURI: Will the Mini ster of CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) the magnitude of diversion of wheat, rice and sugar from the TPDS at 
the national level; 
(b) the reasons therefor 
(c) the steps taken by Government to control such diversion; and 
(d) how far these measures have been effective in controlling diversion of 
foodgrains from TPDS? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI ASHOK 
PRADHAN): (a) and (b) As per a survey conducted by M/s. Tata Ec onomic 
Consultancy Services (TECS) in 1997, the extent of diversion at the national 
level has been estimated at 36% for wheat, 31% for rice and 23% for sugar. 
Many States while recognizing that leak ages do take place, have disagreed 
with the pcrentage of diversion as given in the TECS report. 
The study has highlighted a number of causes of diversion such as existence 
of bogus units, low margins given to Fair Price Shops (FPSs), abnormal 
storage and transit losses in handling by State agencies, irregular supply 
resulting in variation in entitlement, under 
97 

RAJYA SABHA [21 March, 2002] 
measurement, supply of commodities of inferior quality to beneficiaries, lack 
of awareness of entitlement, non-lif ting of commoditites by the upper 
segments of society, etc. 
(c) and (d) The Public Distribution System is implemented under the joint 
responsibility of the Central and State Govemments/UT Addministrations. The 
Central Government is responsible for procurement, storage and transportation of 
the PDS commoditites upto the Central godowns and making them available to 
the States. The responsibility for distribution to the consumers through the Fair 
Price Shops and administration of the PDS rests with the State Governments and 
UT Administrations. State Governments have been requested to closely monitor 
PDS at the FPS and other levels and to make arrangements for distribution of 
PDS commodities in a transparen t and eccountable manner by the 
involvement of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) in the rural areas and local 
bodies in the urban areas. 
In order to streamline the functioning of PDS and make it more accountable and 
effective, Government of India has issued the Public Distribution System (Control) 
Order, 2001 under section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The PDS 
(Control) Order, 2001 contain several piovisions to empower State 
Government/UT Administrations to curb diversion to eliminate bogus ration cards 
and initiate legal action against erring FPS owners, etc. An offence committed 
in violation of the provisions of th e Order invokes criminal liability under 
section 7 of Act.

Smart card system 
1954. SHRI SATISH PRADHAN: 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER  AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Tenth Plan Working Group on Public 
Distribution system and Food Security has recommended introduction of smart-
card system in the form of a credit or debit card instead of the existing ration cards to 
eliminate rampant corruption in PDS in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof alongwith Government's response thereto; 
(c) what steps have been taken or proposed to be taken in this regard; and 
(d) the other recommendations made by the Working Group? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI AS HOK 
PRADHAN): (a) to (c) Yes, Sir. The Tenth Plan Working Group of Planning 
Commission on Public Distribution System and Food Security has recommended 
that the feasibility of the system of food stamps or food credit cards (smart cards) 
may be examined. 
A proposal to introduce smart cards on a pilot basis is under formulation. The 
Planning Commission has allocated an amount of Rs. 4.4 crores in the Annual 
Plan, 2002-2003 for the Pilot Project. 
(d) The other major recommendations of the Working Group are as under:— 
1. Quantum of total food subsidy to be provided, issue price of food grains, 
amount of food grains to be distributed per head, the 
101 

RAJYA SABHA [21 March, 2002] 
extent of subsidy involved in food stamps etc. should be decided by the State 
Governments. 
2. There should be greater decentralization of operations relating to PDS. 
States should be free to procure cereals themselves, buy it from private traders 
or from FCI, and maintain buffer stocks. 
3. The Centre would, however, continue to provide food subsidy. Based on the 
net consumer subsidy spent on providing food through the PDS the Central 
budget should make a provision for national food subsidy. This subsidy would 
be distributed among the States according to a prescribed formula. 
4. In the long run the food subsidy s hould be confined to the population 
below the poverty line. However, for the present, while excess stocks of 
foodgrains exist in FCI godowns, cereals can be supplied under PDS to the 
APL population at a concessional rate as a temporary measure. 
5. It is desirable that the central food subsidy be restricted to two main items 
only namely rice and wheat. 
6. Sugar should be decontrolled and the system of levy on sugar should be 
discontinued. If the government desires lo continue the-sugar subsidy it must 
make an explicit budgetary provision. 
7. The poor should be permitted to buy rations from PDS at more frequent 
intervals at least on a weekly basis. This issue has been addressed in the Public 
Distribution System (Control) Order 2001. 
8. Procurement of foodgrains under relaxed specification of quality should be 
avoided in the future in the interests of well managed public distribution 
system. 
9. The government should discourage the use of ration cards for identification 
purpose. For the purpose of identification multi-purpose identity cards should be 
used as per the control order issued by the food department. 
10. MSP should be at a level that protects the farmer against risk 
of losing money due to collapse of the price of the product. It should 
in most years be allow the market price. 
102 

[21 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
11. Stabilization of cereals prices should continue to be one of the important 
objectives of food policy. This can be acheived through the operation of a 
buffer stock combined with timely intervention by the FCI in domestic 
markets and a liberal import-export policy for foodgrains.

(c) if so, the steps proposed to fortify sugar with vitamin-A to balance the

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI V. SREENIVASA 
PRASAD): (a) The National Institute of Nutritions has informed as under:— 
The Micronutrient deficiencies such as Vitamin-A deficiency, iron deficiency

India. The prevalence of endemic goiter ranges from 10—60% in endemic 
areas. About 1 to 5% of less than of 5 years children exhibit Bitot spots, an

widely prevalent in the country affecting mainly 80—90% of pregnant women, 
adolescent girls and young children.

across the States with States having better investment climate enjoys higher

2008. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY:  Will the Minister of LABOUR

amendments in various labour laws paving the way for the second generation 
of reforms;

Commission set up with the specific job to study and rationalise 
various labour laws in the organise d sectors has been largely rendered 
irrelevant in view of Government's pre-emptive decisions ahead of 
the Commission's recommendations in the matter; and 
153

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (SHRI 
MUNI LALL): (a) and (b) Review/updation of labour laws is a continuous 
process in order to bring them in tune with the prevailing situation and 
emerging needs of the economy. Taking into consideration the requirement of 
productivity, comperitiveness, employment generation and to update the 
provisions of labour laws, a need has been felt to make amendments in 
certain labour legislations and steps initiated accordingly. Thus amendments 
in Trade Unions Act, 1926 and the Workmen's Compensation Act, 1923 were

Payment of subsistence allowance 
†2025. SHRI ABDUL GAIYUR QURESHI: SHRI 
BRATIN SENGUPTA: SHRI VIJAY SINGH 
YADAV: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether payment of subsistence allowance to employees placed under 
suspension is obligatory on the part of Government; 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
171 

RAJYA SABHA [21 March, 2002] 
(b) if so, whether departmental enquiries can be held despite non-payment 
of subsistence allowance; 
(c) if so, whether it is vitiated because of such an instance; 
 
(d) whether Hon'ble Supreme Court has issued instructions in this regard; 
and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, 
PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS (SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA 
RAJE): (a) to (e) Fundamental Rule 53  provides that a Government Servant 
under suspension shall be entitled to the payment of a subsistence allowance. 
The payment of subsistence allowance is a sort of compulsory payment and 
cannot be denied on any ground except when the employee does not furnish a 
certificate that he is not engaged in any other employment, business, profession 
or vocation. In the case of Ghanshyam Das Srivastava Vs. State of Madhya 
Pradesh (AIR 1973 SC 1183), the Supreme Court had observed that where a 
Government Servant under suspension pleaded his inability to attend the 
enquiry on account of financial stringency caused by the non-payment of 
subsistence allowance to him, the proceedings conducted against him ex-
parte would be in violation of the provisions of Article 311(2) of the 
Constitution as the person concerned did not receive a reasonable opportunity 
of defending himself in the disciplinary proceedings. In the light of the above 
mentioned judgement of the Supreme Court, Government have issued 
instructions prescribing that all concerned authorities should take prompt 
steps to ensure that after a Government Servant is placed under suspension he 
receives subsistence allowance without delay.

*244. DR. ALLADI P. RAJKUMAR: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether army authorities have been writing to police authorities to 
ban the use of olive green uniforms by private security agencies in Delhi and 
elsewhere; 
(b) whether certain private security ag encies have started using some 
accessories attached to the military uniforms; 
(c) whether uniforms and above accessori es are freely available in Azad 
Market in Delhi; 
(d) whether militants and other unscrupulous elements made use of the 
uniform items and indulged in nefarius activities; and 
(e) what steps Government propose to take to check the sale of these 
uniform items? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI I.D. SWAMI): (a) to (e) The Government have been alive to the 
security hazards arising out of misuse  of uniforms resembling that of the 
armed or paramilitary forces. Instances where militants/terrorists have used 
uniforms similar to that of the armed/ paramilitary forces have also been 
reported from time to time. The Ministry of Defence have also raised 
concerns in this regard. 
This Ministry has accordingly been advising the State Governments on the 
need to take action under the relevant provisions of law against persons who 
use uniforms similar to the uniforms worn by the military/paramilitary 
forces. 
Provision exist under section 140,170, 171 and 416 of the IPC and section 
6 of the Official Secrets Act for the prosecution of those who use uniforms 
resembling that of the armed forces/paramilitary forces. The proposed 
Private Security Guards and Agencies Regulation Bill, 1994 which is under 
consideration in the Rajya Sabha also has provisions providing for the 
prosecution of private security guards who wear uniforms resembling that, 
army/paramilitary forces. 
No shops selling army uniforms and other accessories have been

*245. DR.  DASARI NARAYANA  RAO:  Will the  Minister  of POWER be 
pleased to state:

and Ramagundam Thermal Power Project in the State of Andhra Pradesh:

Visakhapatnam Thermal Power Project (1040 MW) in Andhra Pradesh being 
promoted by M/s. Hinduja National Power Corporation Limited (HNPCL) has been 
accorded techno-economic clearance of Central Electricity Authority (CEA) on 
July 25, 1996 at an estimated completion cost of USS 943.75 million + Rs. 
1324.993 crores (@ 1 US$ = Rs. 35.00). Counter guarantee of Government of

commence.

Andhra Pradesh (GoAP)/Andhra Pradesh Transmission Corporation 
(APTRANSCO) in the first week of November 1999. The firms financial

F.D.I. in power sector 
*259. SHRI SATISH PRADHAN: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether union government have taken or propose to take any steps for 
increasing Foreign Direct Investment in power sector with a view to eliminate 
the gap between demand and supply of power in the country; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SURESH PRABHU): (a) and (b) The 
policy to attract and encourage greater investment in the power sector through 
private sector participation, including Foreign Direct Investment, was 
announced in 1991 in the background of inability of Government alone to 
mobilize adequate financial resources given the highly capital intensive 
nature of the sector and the large in cremental capacity addition requirements. 
The two part tariff notification issued by Government of India (GoI) on 
30.3.1992 in exercise of powers conferred by sub-section (2) of Section 43A 
of the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948, allows a return of upto 16% on equity 
(paid up and subscribed) at normative levels of operation i.e. 68.5% Plant 
Load Factor (PLF) to generating compan ies in the private sector for power 
projects set up by them. For generation beyond this level, incentive at 
negotiated rates subject to a ceiling of 0.7% of equity (paid up and 
subscribed), for each percentage increas e in PLF is allowed. 100% foreign 
equity participation is permitted in generation, transmission and distribution 
on automatic approval  basis,  without   any  upper limit.  The  Central  
Electricity 
232 

[21 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
Regulatory Commission (CERC) at the Ce ntre as well as State Electricity 
Regulatory Commissions in nineteen States have been set up. The 
Regulatory Commissions will look into all aspects of tariff fixation and 
provide a level playing field for investors. 
In regard to transmission sector, in order to provide comfort to investors, 
the Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd., proposes to obtain all the initial 
clearances such as right-of-way, forest clearances etc. for the projects to be 
offered initially to the private sector. Government has already made the 
enabling legal amendments for facilitating private investment in 
transmission. The regulatory framework is also in position to provide a level 
playing field to all participants. The CERC has issued draft guidelines for 
competitive bidding as well as the terms and conditions for issue of licenses 
to private investors. 
Power distribution is proposed to be privatized on the basis of an area 
approach where under licenses would be  issued for different areas. GoI has 
initiated distribution reforms and has signed Memoranda of Understanding 
with 20 States, under which states have committed for reduction of 
Transmission & Distribution losses, 100% metering, energy auditing etc. In 
turn, GoI have offered to assist the States under the Accelerated Power 
Development Programme (APDP). In the first phase, 63 distribution circles 
in various States have been taken up for intensive upgradation of sub-
transmission and distribution systems. Remaining distribution circles in the 
country would also be taken up for coverage in a phased manner. The 
programme to reduce Transmission & Distribution losses and improvement 
in distribution system would provide considerable opportunities for 
investment as the process of reform and restructuring of  State Electricity 
Boards gains momentum.

Home Minister's Visit to US 
1845. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will th e Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether during his recent visit to the US, he persuaded the US to use 
its influence and ask Pakistan to hand over the terrorists named by India 
including the non-Pakistani criminals; 
(b) if so, the outcome thereof; 
(c) whether the Pak President in his televised address on January 12th, 
made no mention of non-Pakistani terrorists; and 
(d) what steps, if any, have since been asked to extradite them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO): (a) During his visit to 
the US, Home Minister held a co mprehensive dialogue with his US 
interlocutors on the global dimensions of the terrorism. He also articulated 
India's concerns on Pakistan-sponsored cross border terrorism in India and 
Pakistan's role and responsibility in the context of the attack on the 
Parliament of India on 13.12.2001. 
United States has acknowledged that Pakistan must match words by 
action, including with regard to chec king cross border infiltration, taking 
action on the list of 20 fugitives and closing down terrorist organizations in 
Pakistan. 
(c) and (d) Referring to the list of 20 fugitives from law handed over by 
India to Pakistan on 31st December, 2 001, the President of Pakistan, in his 
address to the nation on January 12 stated that there was no question of 
Pakistan handing over any Pakistan national to India. On the presence in 
Pakistan of non-Pakistan nationals who figure on the list of 20 fugitives 
from law, the President sought to obfuscate the issue by stating that Pakistan 
had not give asylum to any such person. 
On 11th February, 2002, India once again called upon the Pakistan 
authorities to take action to apprehend and hand over the individuals 
figuring on the list of 20 fugitives from law. It was also pointed out to 
Pakistan that the authorities of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), 
287

acting as per current international norms, deported to India two individuals 
responsible for the attack on the Am erican Cultural Centre in Kolkata, 
without insisting on time-consuming procedures of extradition, which was very

terrorism.

(c) and (d) Steps taken to reduce transmission and distribution losses 
include:— 
(i) Streamlining  the  power  wheeling/transmission  capability  and 
improving grid discipline. 
(ii) Distribution reforms under the Accelerated Power Development

(vi) Location of low capacity transformers near consumer premises. 
(vii) Installation of shunt capacitors for improvement of power factor.

prevent the losses due to theft of energy:— 
(a). Periodic mass checking drive by vigilance squads as well as field staff.

Reducing dependence on Private Sector for Power 
1862. SHRI SURESH PACHOURI: Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the inflow of private investment targeted during the Ninth Five Year 
plan; 
(b) the actual investment by private sector; 
(c) the reasons for poor response of pr ivate sector in the power sector; 
and 
(d) the measures stipulated to be taken during the Tenth Five Year Plan to 
reduce dependency on private sector? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) Capacity addition during 
9tb plan from private sector was target ed at 17,588 MW. However, the total 
capacity addition in the 9th plan would only be about 5,139 MW. 
(c) while many of the private sector power projects have made substantial 
progress in trying up the various required inputs/ clearances, most of them 
have not been able to achieve financial 
308 

[21 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
cloture. The main reasons for the non-materializaton of these projects are 
mentioned below:— 
(i) The inability of State Electricity Boards (SEBs) and State Governments 
to provide an acceptable payment security. The revenues of the SEBs 
are not adquate to ensure payments to Independent Power producers. 
(ii) Non-fmalisation of various c ontracts such as Power Purchase 
Agreement, Fuel Supply Agr eement and Fuel Transportation 
Agreement acceptable to all the concerned parties. Protracted 
negotiations on fuel prices, liquidated charges/damages, risk-covering 
clauses etc. have caused delays in many cases. 
(iii) High cost of naphtha and other liquid fuels has made the SEBs 
reluctant to buy power from such projects. Nonavailability of gas in 
sufficient quantity has also delaye d progress of projects in some 
states. 
(iv) Court cases in the form of Public Interest Petitions etc. 
(v) Failure by the project developers to bring in equity up front. 
(d) The 9th plan has seen slippages in the targeted capacity addition from 
the private sector as well as State S ector/Central Sector. With the reforms 
process in the power sector now in progress in many of the states, the 
financial condition of the State owned utilities is expected to improve which 
would pave the way for more investments in the private as well as 
Central/State Sector projects. Considering the ambitious programme 
embarked upon by the Government to achieve Tower on Demand' by 2012, 
capacity addition from all sources including private sector is being 
envisaged. In the short run a step up in public sector investment in generation 
has been envisaged from the 10th plan. 
The Accelerated Power Development Programme (APDP) launched by the 
Government aims at revamping the distribution network by better metering, 
billing and collection, reduction of Transmission & Distribution losses and 
theft. This is expected to improve the revenue of SEBs enabling them to pay 
for the additional power capacity and attracting further investments into the 
sector.

Benefit of SGSY to people of Gujarat 
1877. SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to launch any plan of Swarnjayanti 
Gram Swarozgar Yojana; 
(b) if so, the salient feature of the Plan; 
(c) the funds allocated to the Government of Gujarat; and 
(d) the manner in which the Yojana is likely to be beneficial to the people 
of Gujarat? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M. VENKAIAH 
NAIDU): (a) The Swarnjayanti Gram  Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) is 
already under implementation since 1.4.1999. 
(b) The salient features of the Scheme are as under: 
 The SGSY is an integrated programme for Self-Employment of families 
below the poverty line (BPL) in rural areas. 
 It is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme and the financing is shared 
between the Centre and the States in the ratio of 75:25. 
The objective of the Programme is to bring the assisted poor families 
above the poverty line by organising them into Self Help Groups (SHGs) 
through the process of social mobilisation, their training and capacity 
building including skill upgradation and 
324 

[21 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
providing them  income  generating  assets  through   a  mix  of Bank 
Credit and Government Subsidy. 
♦ The Emphasis under the SGSY, is on cluster approach, wherein, 4-5 
dominant activities are identified as Key activities in each block based 
on the local resources, the aptitude as well as the skill of the people and 
the market potentiality. 
♦ The Scheme lays emphasis on the group approach, although individual 
could also be economically assisted. 
♦ Subsidy under the SGSY is uniform at 30% of the project cost, subject 
to a maximum of Rs. 7500. In respect of SC/ STs, however, these will 
be 50% and Rs. 10,000 respectively. For Groups of Swarozgaris 
(SHGs), the subsidy would be at 50% of the cost of the scheme, subject 
to a ceiling of Rs. 1.25 lakh. There will be no monetary limit on subsidy 
for irrigation projects. 
♦ The Scheme provides safeguards for the SCs/STs and weaker section of 
the society. Under the Scheme, 50% of the total swarozgaris assisted 
will be SC/STs, 40% women and 3% disabled. 
♦ Under the Scheme, 10% of the annual allocation is earmarked as 
SGSY-Revolving Fund, 10% as SGSY-Training Fund, 20% (25% in 
case of North-Eastem States) as SGSY-Infrastructure Fund. 
♦ The Swarozgaris assisted under the Scheme are covered for life 
insurance under the Group Life Insurance Scheme for a period of five 
years from the date on which asset is disbursed or sixty years of age, 
whichever is earlier. A sum of Rs. 5,000 is payable by LIC to the 
nominee of deceased in case of natural death and Rs. 10,000 in case of 
death due to accident. 
 
(c) The total Central Allocation for Gujarat under the SGSY. during the 
current year i.e. 2001-2002 is Rs. 1154.96 lakhs. 
(d) The families identified as below poverty line  (BPL) in the 
325

State could be assisted under the Scheme for taking up Self Employment to 
improve their quality of life by way of increased income on sustainable basis.

Conference of International Silk Association in Bangalore 
1889. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of 
TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the four-day World Congress of the International Silk 
Association was held in Bangalore on December 3, 2001; 
(b) if so, what were the main subjects discussed; 
(c) whether the Union Government have announced five point strategy for 
silk industry development; 
(d) if so, the details of the strategy; and 
(e) by when it is likely to be implemented? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
V. DHANANJAY KUMAR): (a) and (b) Yes Sir, International Silk 
Association held its 23rd Congress in Bangalore from 3rd to 6th December, 
2001 to which its members were delega tes. The Congress discussed technical 
as well as trade and market related i ssues. Sessions included the presentation 
of papers by 
337 

RAJYA SABHA [21 March, 2002] 
delegates and discussions in regard to Sericulture and Reeling, Trade in raw 
silk, Trade in silk waste, Trade in thrown silk, Weaving, Trade in silk fabrics, 
silk furnishing, Dyeing, printing and finishing of silk, Technology and 
Research. 
(c) to (e) Government have announced a National Textile Policy which 
lists steps in order to achieve international standard in all varieties of silk. 
The steps include the following five:— 
i. Improving Research & Developmen t and the effective transfer of 
technology at all stages; 
ii. Considerably improving the production of non-mulberry varieties of silk; 
iii. Augmenting efforts for the spread of bivoltine sericulture; 
iv. Encouraging clustering of activities of reeling and weaving and 
strengthen linkages between the producers and industry; 
v. Periodically reviewing the import policy for raw silk taking into account 
the balanced interests of the sericulturists as well as export 
manufacturers.

steps.

1890. SHRI RUMANDLA RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of 
TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the exports of man-made textile have been  hit in recent 
years; 
(b) if so, whether during the year 1996-97, the exports of man-made 
textile showed a decline of 6.5% and during the year 1998-1999, exports of 
these products declined by 12.5% in dollar terms; 
(c) whether during April, 2001, the man-made fabric textile exports 
declined by 8.4 per cent as compared to the corresponding period 
2000; 
(d) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
338 

[21 March, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) the steps being taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI V. 
DHANANJAY KUMAR): (a) to (c) Exports • of man-made textiles declined by 
6.5% in dollar terms during the year 1996-97, however, the exports of man-made 
textiles increased by 14% in dollar terms during the year 1997-98. The exports of 
man-made textiles declined again by 12.5% during 1998-99 in dollar terms. 
However, in 1999-2000 and 2000-2001, the exports of man-made textiles 
increased significantly by 18.8% & 28.1% respectively in dollar terms. Again a 
decline of 8.4% registered during the month of April, 2001 in dollar terms as 
compared to the corresponding month of previous year. 
(d) The slowdown in April is mainly due to general slowdown in economies 
of some of India's major trading partners like the US and increased 
competition from countries like Indonesia, Taiwan, Korea, etc. 
(e) The Government has taken various initiatives to increase exports 
including export of man-made textiles. Some of these measures are: 
i) The Government has de-reserved the woven segment of readymade 
garment from the SSI sector. 
ii) A provision of Rs. 10 crores has been earmarked in the R.E. 2001-02 for 
creating clusters of excellence, i.e. apparel parks for production and 
export of garments. Besides, a provision of Rs. 10 crores has also been 
made in R.E. 2001-02 for scheme for improvement of infrastructure 
facilities at major textile production centres. 
iii) The Technology Upgradation Fund  Scheme (TUFS) has been made 
operational from 1-4-1999 to facilitate the modernisation and 
upgradation of this sector so that it can become more competitive in

pertaining to assistance under TUFS has been constituted.

cotton   for   manufacture   and   export   of ocrapetitive downstream 
textile products.

and Apparel Training & Design Centres (ATDCs) are running

Establishment of Thrift Fund for handloom weavers in Gujarat 
1895. SHRI AHMED PATEL: Will th e Minister of TEXTILES be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether any Thrift Fund has been established in Gujarat for the 
handloom weavers; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the number of weavers being presently covered by the fund in the 
State? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
V. DHANANJAY KUMAR): (a) to (c) The Government of India has been 
implementing the Thrift Fund Scheme since 1985-86 as a social welfare 
measure. The scheme envisages creation of a type of provident fund with 
contribution from the weavers for facilitating them to meet expenses towards 
children's education, medical expenses of family members and expenses in 
connection with marriage and other re ligious ceremonies. The contribution 
under this scheme is being shared @8% of the wages earned by the weaver 
and 4% each by the Central and the State Governments. This scheme is 
implemented in the country including in the State of Gujarat. During 2000-
01, 3171 weavers of Gujarat have been covered under this scheme.

Centra] Health Package Scheme for handloom weavers in Gujarat 
1898. SHRI AHMED PATEL: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Central Health Package Scheme for handloom weavers is 
under implementation in Gujarat; and 
(b) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
V. DHANANJAY KUMAR): (a) and (b) Yes,  Sir; the Government of India 
has been implementing the Health Package Scheme for the handloom 
weavers in the country including the State of Gujarat. Under the scheme, 
assistance is provided towards cost of reimbursement of medicines upto Rs. 
1500/- per weaver per annum for treatment of Tuberculosis, Asthma and 
inflammation of alimentary system; and cost of spectacles limited to Rs. 
150/- and eye-testing limited to Rs. 40/- per weaver; maternity benefit in the 
form of lump-sum grant to women weavers or women belonging to weavers' 
households @ Rs. 500/- per woman per delivery, twice in her life-time; and 
monetary incentive at the rate of Rs. 100/- per head to each handloom 
weavers/his or her spouse, who undertakes permanent measures for family 
planning. Besides this, in order to provide potable drinking water, assistance 
of Rs. 35,000/-per bore well is provided for every 50 weavers households 
and up to Rs. 1.00 lakh for providing in frastructure for each of the primary 
health care centres in areas having a concentration of weaver population. An 
amount of Rs. 55.11 lakh was released to the State of Gujarat during the year 
2000-01 under the Health Package Scheme.

Security matters concerning Railways 
DR. RAJA RAMANNA (Nominated): Sir, the Railways are the most 
susceptible system to te rrorist attacks unless more than ordinary precautions 
are taken against such attacks. They carry important freight and personnel to 
the border areas that are infested by te rrorists or their supporters. Security 
methods, involving electronic methods, are well known, and it is our hope that 
they are fully utilized. I, however, wish to  bring to the attention of the Railways 
that in spite of warnings by this H ouse, no attention has been paid to the 
insecurity to the trains due to the unrestricted growth of slums along the 
railway lines stretching far out from many important city stations. 
In recent years, houses have been built all along the railway lines but 
at a distance considered safe by the authorities. But the space in between 
these houses and the railway lines is occupied by slum-dweller, who are poor 
people. It would be easy for a terrorist to hide in these areas and push a bomb 
or other lethal material into a train or on to the railway tracks.  Therefore, it is 
necessary that these extensive settl ements on railway property are removed 
immediately. The need for railway security must be stressed for removing 
these unlawful constructions which are not only a sad sight to tourists, but also 
a place" of immediate danger to ou r fighting forces, in particular, and 
passengers, in general. 
Need to solve Mullaiperiar Dam issue 
SHRI S. AGNI RAJ (Tamil Nadu): I rise to make a Special Mention on 
the need to solve the Mullaiperiar Dam issue in Tamil Nadu. The 107-year-old 
Periar Dam, built by Er. Benny Cook, has been the source of irrigation for the 
rain-fed regions of Madurai and Rama nathapuram. Though the height of the 
dam is 159 feet, Tamil Nadu was allowed to store water up to 152 feet, for the 
purpose of irrigation. First, in 19 73, and, again in 1978, the Kerala 
Government expressed apprehensions about the safety of the dam. Following 
the advice of the Expert Committee and the Central Water Commission, the 
Tamil Nadu Government had spent crores of rupees to strengthen the dam. 
But the Kerala Government did not allow Tamil Nadu to store water beyond 
136 feet. More than 50 TMC feet of water of Mullaiperiar River is running 
waste into the sea.   But the southern districts of 
377

democracy. But it is painful that a si ster State is violating a 99-year-old

has not been protected. There is widespread disappointment over this in Tamil 
Nadu. The Centre should not drag on this issue any further. It should direct the 
Government of Kerala to allow Tamil Nadu to store water in the Mullaiperiar

(SECOND) ORDINANCE, 2001 AND THE PREVENTION OF TERRORISM 
BILL, 2002. 
SHRI KAPIL SIBAL (Bihar):   Sir, I move:- 
"That this House disapproves the Prevention of Terrorism (Second) 
Ordinance, 2001 (No.12 of 2001) promulgated by the President on 
the 30th December, 2001". 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, this House is aw are of the fact that as far back 
as October 15, 2001, the first Ordinance in  respect of prevention of terrorism 
was promulgated. This House is also  aware of the fact that this was 
promulgated immediately after the events of Septembe r 11, 2001, when 
everybody knew that the House was to assemble on the I9 th of November, 
2001. The Government was aware of t he fact that the House was to meet; 
and,   on   a   sensitive   matter  like  this.   I   would   have  thought  that  the 
392   . 

[21 MARCH, 2002]                      RAJYA SABHA 
Government would take the Opposition into confidence, hold consultations, 
and, during the course of the Session, move an appropriate piece of 
legislation so that it would be acceptable to all. I say this not only on behalf of 
my party; I believe, I am expressing the sentiments of this House; nobody in 
this House or outside does not wish t hat terrorism should be fought in the 
strongest possible terms. I think this nat ion is committed to fighting terrorism, 
and nobody should have two opinions on that. We are only concerned at the 
mode and the manner in which such a draconian piece of legislation is being 
pushed by this Government, without regard to the sentiments of large sections 
of society which have expressed serious concerns about the efficacy of this 
law. Yet, today, this is a defining moment in history when the people of this 
country have to take a position; political parties in this country have to take a 
position. We tried very hard, Sir, to ent er into a dialogue with the Government. 
Indeed, today itself, I moved an amendm ent to the Bill; under rule 125, I 
sought the reference of this Bill to a Select Committee of this House. What 
was the purpose of this move? The purpose of this move was, let us sit 
together; let us look at some  of the provisions; let us have a dialogue; let us 
explain to you which provisions we think might not be efficacious; let us also 
add certain provisions so that all those who perpetrate terrorism, whether it is 
State-perpetrated terrorism or otherwise, are brought within the ambit of this 
Bill. But, I am sorry to say, Sir, -- this was an escape route that we gave to the 
Government -- there was no move by t he Government, in fa ct, to meet us 
even half way. This proposal was re jected outright. Unfortunately, this 
particular amendment was moved today, which, under the rules, ought to have 
been moved before 24 hours, and we sought the permission of the Chair to 
waive the period of notice. Unfortunately, the Government has not cooperated. 
So, it cannot be said that from our si de, from our point of view, we have not 
tried to meet with you, tried to discuss  the law with you, so that we give a 
humane face to this draconian piece of l egislation. Having said that, Sir, I go 
back to what I had said earlier, we are st anding, today, at the turning point of 
the history of this country, when peopl e and political parties have to make 
choices. In fact, I am reminded of the words of the second President of the 
United States, John Adams, when, on 23 rd March, 1776, he wrote to Horatio 
Gates, and said, "I agree with you that in politics, the middle way is none at 
all." Yes, there are moments when middl e ways are none at all. You have 
heard President Bush's State of the Union Address, in which he said, "either 
you are with us or you are against us." So , either we are for this Bill or we are 
against this Bill. You have chosen

RAJYA SABHA [21 MARCH, 2002]  
your way, and we, I believe, have chosen ours. You seek to sacrifice civil 
liberties, in the national interest; we seek to protect civil liberties, in the 
national interest; you seek to combat terrorism through law; we seek to 
combat a law that perpetuates State terro rism; you seek to divide an already 
fractious polity; we seek to unite a fr actious nation; you seek to unlearn from 
the past; we seek to learn from the past. You have chosen your way, and we 
have chosen ours. 
Sir, one of the issues that we hav e been raising in the public, time 
and again, is that, if you have this law in place, in the hands of an enforcement 
authority, which has no regard for human rights and which acts at the instance 
and under the direction of State authority, then the ordinary, innocent, people of 
this country will be victims of this law. Sir, I am sorry to say that just as we 
have spoken, these words came true, because the proof of the pudding is 
ultimately in the eating. If you remember, Sir, it was in November, 2001 when, 
for the first time, POTO was put into force in Jammu and Kashmir. In other 
words, the first arrest in Jammu and Kashmir took place under POTO was in 
November. And what happened? A family, which had nothing to do with 
terrorism, its entire property was attached. There was a public outcry. The 
Government, the Law Minister of the State of Jammu and Kashmir had to 
make a statement publicly. "This is a gr oss misuse of the law." This was the 
first instance of the use of POTO in Jammu and Kashmir itself. 
But, Sir, let us come nearer home an d to recent events. I only invite 
the attention of this Government to wh at happened in Gujarat; and I invite the 
attention of the Government to a report published in the Indian Express just the 
other day, when we were told that 62 persons of a particular community were 
arrested by the Gujarat Government for the Godhra carnage, and that all 62 of 
them were booked under POTO. Well, Sir, if they are responsible for these 
crimes, we have no objection. Indeed,  the law must take its course and 
anybody, who is responsible for the carn age at Godhra, must be dealt with in 
the strongest possible terms. We have no two opinions on that. But, Sir, look at 
what happened to those who perpetrated the violence in Ahmedabad and 
other towns in Gujarat thereafter. 
We had the very unfortunate Kargil episode, in which those from 
across the border came into our territory and we lost very precious lives, we 
lost over 500 lives in Kargill. But this co untry must also know that the lives lost 
in Gujarat were more than 500, more than the total number of lives lost

using POTO on a selective basis. I invi te the attention of the hon. Home 
Minister to a newspaper report. It is stated that in Ahmedabad city alone, 
according to the official police figures, besides 300 deaths, 1679 houses were

burnt, 200 shops were looted and 90 vehicles were torched. Sir, this is in 
Ahmedabad alone. 
In a FIR lodged by the Sub-Inspector, Shri B.K. Solanki, of the 
Naroda Police Station, named five VHP and Bajarang Dal leaders of the 
Naroda-Patia massacre. Among them is the Bajarang Dal activist, Babu 
Bajrangi, who has a long criminal record. Three persons have so far been 
arrested but those named in the FIR are still at large. 
Forget about POTO. They are not  even sought to be arrested and 
this FIR is not lodged by an ordinary person on the street, but it was lodged by 
the Sub-Inspector of the Naroda Police Station. The Assistant Commissioner 
of Police, Mr. Bharot, who is given the charge of the invest igation, questions 
the action of the local police. In other words, the ACP is questioning the action 
of the Sub-Inspector of Police, who has lodged the FIR. And what is he 
saying? He is saying that before any a rrest of Bajrangi and others named in

pudding is in the eating. This is the actual working of the POTO at the ground 
level. The State machinery has co llaborated to protect those who ex facie are 
terrorists. Further I ask you: What is  terrorism? You have defined it in the 
POTO. What does it say? It says that if any section of society is terrorised by 
acts of others and in that process, inju ries are caused either to the person or 
property, then he falls within the definition of a terrorist act. Nobody can say

terror when people were burnt alive, ju st as the carnage of Godhara was an 
act or terror where people were burnt alive? So, these were acts of terror.   
Yet despite the fact that these were acts of terror, far

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (SHRI ADHI K SHIRODKAR): Mr. Subbian. 
Sir, you have eight minutes, and please allow me to stick to the schedule.

SHRI KA. RA. SUBBIAN (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I thank you for having 
given me this opportunity to offer my remarks on this Bill. 
In all spheres of human activity, the basic requirements are justice, 
equality, fairness and impartiality. Fund amental right is the right of every 
human being. The Fundamental Rights ar e guaranteed in the Constitution. 
The substantial law and the procedural law have to be complied with, before 
initiating any proceedings of penal nat ure. But, in India, ever since 1955, 
several enactments, which infringe and violate the Fundamental Rights of the 
citizens of India, on the ground of su ppressing terrorism, have been enacted. I 
need not spell out all the Acts. But, some  of these are the National Security 
Act, 1980, the Armed Forces Special Powers Act, 1958, the Disturbed Areas 
Act, the Unlawful Activities (Preventi on) Act, 1967, and so on.   There are 
several such Acts. 
Lastly, we had seen the TADA and the MISA. TADA and MISA were 
laws that affected more the rights of human beings. Under MISA, we were the 
worst sufferers. Our hon. Minister of Commerce and Industry, Shri Murasoli 
Maran, was detained. The hon. Member, Sh ri P. N. Siva, who is sitting here, 
was taken into custody and was detained while he was just 21 years old. 
Without assigning any reason, more than 500 people were kept under 
detention. Under TADA also, more than 75,000 people were arrested 
throughout the country and put behind th e bars. Hardly about one per cent of 
the arrestees were convicted. Now, we have this POTO. What is the necessity 
for bringing POTO? This has to be seen. We have, before us, an enactment to 
deal with the menace of terrorism. We do not have any law against terrorism 
and terrorists. This is an important piece of legislation because it concerns the 
dignity and integrity of this country. 
What has happened during the la st 15 years? The menace of 
terrorism has taken the valuable lives of  almost 61,000 civilians, the lives of 
8000 untiring Army personnel and policemen.   Almost 6,00,000 people have 
444 

[21 MARCH, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
Deen rendered homeless because of terrorism in various parts of our country. 
About Rs. 45,000 crores have been spent for tackling insurgency. There is no 
stringent law in our country to tackle terro rism. Terror is meant to inflict fear in 
the minds of others. We see the lightni ng speed with which terrorists, persons 
involved in disruptive activities, as also  those wanting to create problems in 
the country, have been operating. That is why a sharp, precise and quick 
enforcement of the law is required. Ther e is an upsurge in terrorist activities, 
intensification of cross-border terrorist activities, and insurgency, in dilferent 
parts of the country. Terrorism, in general , has acquired global dimension and 
has become a challenge for the entire world. In their reach and the methods 
adopted by them, the terrorist groups  and organisations take advantage of 
modern means of communication technology, using high-tech facilities 
available, in the form of communicati on system, transport, sophisticated arms 
and various other means. The existing criminal justice system is not designed 
to deal with the type of heinous crimes which the proposed law deals with. 
That is why the Hon. Home Minister has brought POTO. The Central 
Government as well as the State Governments can implement this law. 
Sir, now, I would like to draw the attention of the Home Minister to 
clause 4(b). Sir, clause 4(b) of the Bill states, 'Where any person is in 
unauthorised possession of any - bombs, dynamite or hazardous explosive 
substances or other lethal weapons capab le of mass destruction or biological 
or chemical substances of warfare in any area, whether notified or not,..." he 
can be punished. Sir, my submission is, this provision of the law will be used 
by the police to implicate innocent pers ons. It will be used by the police very 
easily. The police will plant a country-made bomb or some gelatine stick or a 
weapon and arrest a citizen. A stage-made drama will be enacted, as if it was 
recovered from the person. If he is arre sted, he will not be entitled for bail for 
one year. If the offence is proved, by producing false writings, he will be 
sentenced to three years' imprisonment or life imprisonment. This is a very 
draconian law. Some amendments are necessary, as far as the definition in 
clause 4(b) is concerned. Even a ganja can be planted and a false case can 
be foisted against any person. 
Sir, many senior Members of this august House have said in detail 
about confession recorded by a police officer. As per clause 32(1) of the Bill, 
the confession made before a police officer, not lower in rank than a 
Superintendent of Police, shall be admissi ble in trial. Sir, my submission is, 
under section 25 of the Evidence Act, the confession cannot be recorded by 
445 

RAJYA SABHA [21 MARCH, 2002]  
a police officer. As submitted by my friend just now, under section 27 of the 
Evidence Act, confession made before a police officer is admissible, subject to 
recovery of any facts or material. So, as per sections 25 and 27 of the 
Evidence Act, confessions made before a Superintendent of Police are not 
admissible as evidence. Whereas, if the confession is recorded by the 
Superintendent of Police, under this Bill,  it is admissible as evidence. It is a 
great anomaly. How can it be accepted? How can it be acted upon? 
Sir, when the TADA case was challenged in the Supreme Court, a 
three-judge bench held that confessi on made before a police officer, under 
TADA, is admissible. Justice K. Ramasa my and Justice Sahai observed that it 
was not admissible as evidence. They observed that there is a difference 
between the confession made before a judicial officer and the confession 
recorded by a police officer. It is due to their very character. They have 
observed that there is a basic differ ence between the approach of a police 
officer and a judicial officer. A judicial officer is trained and tuned to reach the 
truth, by a fair procedure. A police officer is trained to achieve the result, 
irrespective of the means that are employ ed. So long as the goal is achieved, 
the means are irrelevant, as far as a police officer is concerned. Whether he is 
a constable or a Superintendent of Po lice, the problem does not lie in the 
personnel, but in the culture. Unless t he police culture is changed, it will 
always be difficult to rely on the confession recorded by the police. 
Sir, the accused has to be produc ed, within 48 hours, before the 
magistrate, and the magistrate can record  the statement of the accused. As a 
practising lawyer, not only as a public prosecutor, but also as a defence 
lawyer, I can say that none of the a ccused will complain against the police 
when he is produced from the custody of the police. What I want is that the 
accused should be kept in judicial custody, and 24 hours time should be given 
to them to admit or not to admit the genuineness of the statement recorded by 
the police. However, the confession recorded by the police officer should not 
be final. It should be recorded in the presence of two independent and reliable 
witnesses. Sir, as far as the criminal procedure is concerned, we have got 
provisions-sections 436, 437, 438 and 439. 436 is bailable, 437 and 439 are 
non-bailable and 438 relates to anticipatory bail. As far as this Bill is 
concerned, enormous powers have been gi ven to the Public Prosecutors. 
What does it say? "If the Public Prosec utor opposes the bail application, then 
the accused can't be granted bail." There should be some amendment to 
clause 49 of this Bill. Unfettered powers should not be 
446 

[21 MARCH, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
given to the Public Prosecutors, because we know how the Public 
Prosecutors, nowadays, are acting. Without any reason, they may oppose the 
application. We have the genesis of th is kind of law in England, during the 
War years. 
Here, there is a provision, cl ause 37, for appointing Competent 
Authority. As far as the States are co ncerned, the Secretary should be made 
the Competent Authority; as far as the Centre is concerned, the Joint Secretary 
should be made the competent authority, to whom powers be given. As I said, 
we have the genesis of this kind of law in England during the war years When 
England was facing an attack or an aggression by foreign forces, a near civil 
war situation arose in the country, wi th the connivance of some foreign 
elements. Prevention of Detention Act was conceived in 1944, during the 
Second World War. About 200 people were put behind the bar. It was the 
Secretary of Home who had ordered the arrests. 
Now, in our country under the proposed law, under clause 37, 
Secretaries to the Government of various  States are given orders to file the 
cases. I suggest that this power shou ld be vested only with the Union Home 
Ministry, to avoid misuse and its abuse. When we continue to follow the 
British system, from the days of McCaulay, there is nothing wrong in following 
this provision. 
My appeal is, the Prevention of Terrorism law must be subject to 
review by Parliament every year, on th e basis of a report submitted by the 
Review Committee to the Parliament, as far as every detainee is concerned. 
This law should be withdrawn, if the object is not complied with. There should 
be a wider discretion to the judge to grant  bail. There should be a strict time 
frame for trial, as far as the disposal of the cases are concerned. Just as in 
sessions cases, the trial of the case should be made day-to-day. 
The Centre should be vigilant and t he States should be kept under 
strict observation so that no State misuses or abuses the provisions of the law 
against the leaders of any political party, to wreck vengeance against them. 
The States should be kept under observat ion, for any misuse or abuse. With 
these words, I conclude. Thank you.

"Giving due weight to all the considerat ions indicated above, we have come to 
the conclusion that section I5(2)(b) cannot be upheld and falling within the

Sir, this is very important. 
"Without allowing the grounds of such imposition, both in their factual 
and legal aspects, to be duly tested in  judicial inquiry is a strong element 
which in our opinion must be taken into account in judging the relevance of the 
restrictions imposed by Section 52 of  the Act". Than they say, "No summary 
and what is bound to be largely one-sided review by an Advisory Board even 
where its verdict is binding on the executive Government, can be a substitute 
for a judicial inquiry". Now the same enactment was again considered in the 
year 1995 and the Supreme Court again said, "Unless you have a judicial 
inquiry, the Act cannot be upheld". My  submission before the House is, let us 
not enact a law which takes away your right under article 19(1) (c) of the 
Constitution. 
Now let us examine clause 18 of the Bill. If we read clause 18, it does 
not give any reasons on the basis of wh ich an association is sought to be 
banned. How do you expect a member of an organisation to make a 
representation to you for the purpose of a review and when the review is 
allowed, there is no clear cut authority? It has to be by a judicial authority 
which has to decide whether there are sufficient grounds on the basis of which 
you are seeking to ban a particular organisation. If we go back to the Act of 
1967, look at Sections 3 and 4.   Section 3 very clearly indicates

that a notification can be issued specifying the grounds on the basis of which a 
particular organisation could be declared as unlawful. You are giving a chance 
of being heard to the party concerned to  represent before the authority. It is 
obligatory on the Government to place the notification before the court and the 
court has to take a decision. In ordinary circumstances, the notification is not 
valid, is not effective till it is confirmed by a sitting judge of the High Court. Now 
what is the position of hearing? You do not have any provision for deciding the 
matter in a judicial inquiry by a sitting judge of the High Court. Clause 16 says 
that either you may have a sitting ju dge or a retired judge and their two 
members on the left and right. The two members on the left and right can 
overrule either the sitting judge or the retired judge of the High Court. My 
submission before the House is that these two provisions are totally ultra vires 
the Constitution which have already been held to be so in the year 1952. 
My next point is regarding the right of privacy which has been 
conferred by article 21 of the Constitu tion. All countries of the world including 
America have an enactment called the Electronic Communication Privacy Act 
of 1986. These powers have been given to a judge, to a judicial authority. 
Before you do a wire tapping, you have to apply before a judge and the judge 
after hearing the petitioner gives the author ity to the particular individual to 
start recording. Here what you have done is, the right of privacy has been 
taken away. We have a judgement of 1996 of the Supreme Court in which they 
said, "You can give authority for wire tapping on sufficient grounds and that 
authority will not be the investigating officer. The information which will be 
given to the investigating officers will be limited to the part of investigation 
which he is supposed to do". You kindly see what is sought to be done in 
clause 42 of the present enactment. It says. "An interception under this 
Chapter may be conducted in whole or in part by a public servant, acting under 
the supervision of the investigating officer authorised to conduct the 
interception". You are giving all kinds of powers to the police officer. I must 
remind you as to what was said before this House on 11 May 1989 by Shri 
Yashwant Sinha. He said, "A constable in London enjoys far greater credibility 
then your Director-General of Police here . Do not provoke me to say anything 
more." What you are doing here is that  you are giving all the powers to the 
police authorities to wire-tap. Wire-tapping is a very serious matter which 
infringes upon the fundamental right to privacy. Your talks on telephone are 
very private in nature. And, this is a very serious matter which cannot be taken 
lightly. Mr. Sinha further said, "I have no doubt, as Mr. Malaviya said, if Gandhi 
or

Sir, the third objection which I have is, as regards clause 49. I feel that 
there is something wrong in this claus e. I understand that clause 49 (5) says 
that there is no provision for an anticipatory bail. Ther e is no problem about it. 
But, look at sub-clause (6). It says: "Notwithstanding anything contained in the 
Code, no person accused of an offence punis hable under this Act shall, if in 
custody, be released on bail or on his own bond unless the Court gives the 
Public Prosecutor an opportunity of bei ng heard"; meaning thereby that before 
the bail is to be granted, a notice has to  be given to the Public Prosecutor. 
Okay; fair enough. But there is also a proviso to it -- this proviso is very 
relevant - which says: "Provided that afte r the expiry of a period of one year 
from the date of det ention of the accused for an offence under this Act, the 
provisions of sub-clause (6) of this se ction shall apply"; meaning thereby that 
this sub-clause will apply after completion of one year. So, there is no provision 
in the Bill for the first one year. Now, if we read this sub-clause and the proviso 
together, do we take it that for a peri od of one year, we cannot go before the 
Prosecutor? And, as per this sub- clause, the man would be kept under 
detention without any hearing. 
So, Sir, in view of the above-said lapses, I cannot support this Bill.

militants and the militants could esca pe very easily. This happened before  
1991. After 1991, our dynamic leader came to power in Tamil Nadu. She 
banned the LTTE and the Tamil militants. When the hon. Home Minister went 
to Coimbatore to attend a meeting, the te rrorists tried to assassinate him. Two 
great leaders of India, Shrimati Indira  Gandhi and Shri Rajiv Gandhi were also

assassinated by the LTTE in Tamil Nadu. Sir, our neighbouring country is 
indulging in terrorist activities through the ISI and other agencies in the 
Kashmir Valley and in the North Eastern Region which is creating communal 
disharmony. They are also spreading rumours which are creating confusion 
and they trying to dislodge the secular and democratic fabric of our country. 
Sometime back, terrorists attacked the Jammu Assembly and killed 
many innocent people. 
Sir, our leader has always kept t he terrorists under leash. So far as 
Kashmir is concerned, the terrori sts unleshed by the ISI have not only 
destroyed the peace but they have also  destroyed the ec onomy of the State 
which is described as the heaven on earth because of its greenery. The ISI is 
trying to persuade, cajole and threaten the youth of this country to take to the 
path of terrorism and they are trying to turn them against the country. In these 
circumstances, we should have a stringent law like the POTO in order to 
prevent terrorism. This is the right time when we should enact such legislation. 
The argument given by the Opposit ion parties which are opposing 
this legislation is that even when the PO TO is in existence, such incidents are 
still taking place.   I would like to put a simple question to these parties.

The Indian Penal Code is in existence,  but still people are being murdered.

misused. There is a possibility that such exceptional power to curb terrorism 
might be misused by a few people. 
But the affected can approach the Court and get remedy. Sir, many 
laws in the statute book are being misused. As a lawyer, I have seen in many

Maharashtra, where the Congress (I) is in power, have similar laws operating

also look at the merits and the contents of the law. Today, terrorism is limited 
not just to India, but  it has become a global phenomenon. In every 
international conference, tenorism is being discussed. Every country is 
persuaded to bring a law like POTO to c heck terrorism. With the existing laws, 
it takes years to bring to book the criminals, and the criminals also get 
acquitted easily, without a law like POTO. I would like to add that merely 
having a law is not sufficient, but the law enforcing authority should be able to 
tackle these activities effectively. These days, when the terrorists are using 
modern, sophisticated weapons like AK-47s, and are killing innocent people, 
and even the VIPs, we are all the time under the threat from these terrorists. In 
this connection, I would like to impress upon the Government the need to 
allocate adequate funds for complete modernisation of the police force. Tamil 
Nadu has a special problem. It has a coastline of thousand kilometres, which 
is 13 per cent of the national coastline. So, special attention should be given to

Government  will  lend  a  helping  hand  by allocating adequate funds  for

senior advocates and are legal luminaries, have spoken about it. This is 
regarding withholding copies of the st atement given by witnesses against the

Government should do that. Whatever may be the crime, till it is proved in the 
court, the accused is deemed to be innocent, under the law. Copies of 
statements of witnesses and the addresses of witnesses should be supplied to 
the accused. Otherwise, it would be against natural justice and also in violation 
of article 20(3) of the Constitution. So far as clause 32 pertaining to confessions

the Indian Evidence Act is considered to  be the best enactment in the whole 
world. It says very specifically that a statement made against oneself is against 
the law of natural justice. In the pr oposed Bill, a confession made before a 
police officer can be admissible, and it w ill be adequate to convict that person.

In India, the environment is totally different. The police authorities, many a time, 
extract confessions from people under duress; it has become a practice.

abused like the TADA. As was pointed out by many Members, TADA was

liberties.

prosecutor. So, my request is that this provision of the Bill should be modified.

In no uncertain terms, I would say that if this Bill is enacted, it will encourage 
further irresponsible and brutal policing; the police will harass, victimise and 
intimidate innocent people through unwarranted detention and coercion. This 
would further damage the existing legal system, denigrate modern 
.jurisprudence and strike at the very basis of the civil society. 
I do not agree that POTO is a clone or an exact replica of TADA. It is 
significantly worse than even TADA, as its scope extends beyond terrorists, to 
terrorist organisations and sympathisers or supporters who are not necessarily 
terrorists, by definition. This is the mo st egregious feature of this Bill, because 
anybody will be termed as a supporter of terrorism, and that way, the 
Government, the police, will settle their personal scores or political scores. 
POTO is the most harsh and dehumanised form of a preventive law which will 
invariably be used to thwart he voice of protest, the voice of dissent; I repeat it 
once again. I would like to give one or  two examples, even at the cost of 
repetition. Clause 32(1) is quite horrifying,  to the extent that an officer of the 
rank of the Superintendent of Police is empowered to extract confessions from 
the accused and present those as evid ence. This ominous provision has not 
only the potential for abuse; this, in itself, is directly abusive. I say that I am not 
worried about the abuse of POTO.    But I am anxious about the use of POTO.    
POTO will be used 
507 

RAJYA SABHA [21 MARCH. 2002|  
barbarously, with a mala fide intention, to silence the voice of dissent. It has 
been widely commented by many distinguished legal luminaries and hon. 
Members like Kapil Sibal and many others have already pointed out and 
commented on the legal problems that  are going to emerge out of POTO. I 
would say, once again, that I have raised it on a number of times in this House, 
that the breeding grounds of terrorism ha ve to be taken care of. The poverty 
has to be taken care of. The unemployment problem has to be taken care of. 
The social alienation has to be taken care of. Unless we address these issues, 
we will not be able to succeed, in spite of having POTO or even if some other 
dreaded, draconian laws are brought. I would once again say that I was 
provoked at one time when Shri L.K. Advani was asking, 'Whether you doubt 
our bona fides.' Yes, Sir. We doubt their bona fide. We doubt the bona fides of 
this Government. It has been clearly es tablished that this Government has 
acted in the most mala fide manner on many occasions and they have tried to 
intimidate, harass as well as discriminat e against the minorities, and that is 
why we doubt the bona fides of this Government. If this sort of Bills are passed 
in this House, if the police is empo wered with more powers, the present 
irresponsible police, whose mindset is still the feudal mindset, even pre-
colonial mindset, will, definitely, misuse this POTO or misuse this sort of 
enactments. I am sure, this Government, the treasury benches, will consider

serious and don't think that you can do justic e with this sort of Bill. This sort of

With these words, I once again appeal to the Government to 
withdraw this Bill and make necessary arrangements for a decent settlement

SHRI FALI S. NARIMAN (Nominated): Sir, when I was much younger 
at the bar, I appeared, for the firs t time, before a Bench of 11 judges, 
constituted for the first time, in the Gola k Nath case. I recall that after one side 
had spoken, and the other side had also  spoken, there was an advocate who 
stood up and said, "My lord, now I am last.   I will either 
508 

[21 MARCH, 2002] RAJYA SABHA  
hit out or get out." Sir, I propose to hit out. I would like to make a few points - 
there is not much time for speeches; there is time only for points -- as to why I 
oppose this Bill. One, we do not need it. We already have the National 
Security Act that permits Central and State Governments to preventively 
detain persons who are a danger to the se curity of the State, and 'terrorists' 
are, by definition, a danger to the secu rity of the State. The Home Minister 
may tighten up its provisions. Expand i t, if he wishes, but let us not have 
another harsh law. We already have one. It has already been constitutionally 
upheld by the Supreme Court. Second;  preventive detention of suspected 
terrorists is easier to administer, since it does not involve pr osecution, trial or 
extracting confessions to establish proof. This is precisely what Great Britain 
has done. After a very stormy debate in the English Parliament, it very 
recently, only in February, enacted the Antiterrorism and Crime Act. And, what 
does it provide for? No prosecution and trial like in POTO, but indefinite 
detention, without charge, of non-British nationals, reasonably suspected by 
the Home Secretary to be involved in terrorist acts, somewhat like in our 
National Security Act. The UK, I believe has correctly addiessed itself to the 
ground realities of terrorism. The problem with terrorist activities, howsoever 
defined, is the intrinsic difficulty of proof in a court of law. That is why we could 
not try Omar Sheikh in a TADA Court, who had been preventively been 
detained in the J&K for nearly five years, till he was released in exchange for 
the Indian Airlines hostages, in Kandahar, lnere was great suspicion of his 
involvement in terrorist acts, but there was no proof that could stand in the 
court of law. President Musharraf said as much, when he tried to discredit the 
Government of India before the internatio nal media, when confronted with the 
abduction and murder by the same Omar Sheikh of Daniel Pearl, an American 
correspondent of the Wall Street Journal. Thirdly, Sir, because there are better 
safeguards in our Prevent ive Detention Law, than in POTO. The Advisory 
Board, mandated by article 22, consisting of High Court judges, has to review 
every detention every three months. All you require is to bring into force, which 
no Government has brought into force since 1978, the Constitution Forty-Forth 
(Amendment) Act, which is, that the Advi sory Board must consist of sitting 
judges not retired judges, because of the confidence of the public in the 
established courts with sitting judges . Sir, another thing is, that POTO was 
much harsher than the present Bill and was in force on December 13 th, but it 
could not prevent the worst terrorist atta ck that we had on our Parliament. The 
POTO could not save us. It was only our brave security personnel who did.    
Lastly, I oppose the Bill 
509 

RAJYA SABHA [21 MARCH, 2002]  
because although its provisions were recommended by the Law Commission, 
a non-statutory body, as stated by the hon. Home Minister in his opening 
statement, the National Human Right s Commission has firmly expressed its 
opinion against it, and even after its amendment, it has opposed it. And, who 
leads the National Human Rights Commission? Former Chief Justice of India, 
Mr. Verma, who delivered the majority judgement in the Ayodhya case. Need 
hon. Members listen to contentious lawyers in this House, expressing differing 
opinions and get more confused especially when a former Chief Justice of 
India as the head of statut ory body, established by Parliament, had refused to

has his Government done to allay the co ncerns of the National Human Rights 
Commission? Sir, I believe, in the absenc e of consensus amongst all political 
parties, the POTO should never have b een pressed. These are my reasons 
why I oppose the Bill.   Thank you.
